title: Young People and Politics
objective: After this level you can describe ways young people take part before they can vote.
summary: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child gives children a right to be heard. Youth parliaments, letters to representatives and volunteering are ways in before voting age.

cards.headline: In 2009, teenagers took over the green benches of the House of Commons.
cards.body: On 30 October 2009, about 300 Members of the UK Youth Parliament debated in the Commons chamber. It was the first time a group other than MPs had used it. So what can you do in politics before you're old enough to vote?

cards.headline: A right to be heard
cards.body: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 1989, is the world's most widely ratified human rights treaty. It counts everyone under 18 as a child, unless the law sets adulthood earlier. Its Article 12 gives a child capable of forming views the right to express them freely in all matters affecting them, given due weight for age and maturity. Too young to vote isn't too young to be heard.

cards.headline: Practice parliaments
cards.body: Youth parliaments turn that right into a habit. In the UK Youth Parliament, any young person aged 11 to 18 can vote or stand, members are elected, and once elected they run campaigns on issues that matter to young people. It's the real machinery in miniature. You learn politics the way you learn to swim: by getting in.

mascot.line: Candidates, ballots, campaigns: same moves, smaller pool.

cards.headline: Tools that don't need a ballot
cards.body: This chapter has already handed you two more. Level 93: a UK MP represents all the people who live in the constituency, not only voters, so your letter counts. Level 94: volunteering is unpaid, non-compulsory work that anyone can choose to give. Neither one asks to see a voter card.

cards.headline: Young people: heard
learned: The Convention on the Rights of the Child: a right to be heard
Its Article 12 covers all matters affecting children
UK Youth Parliament: elected members aged 11 to 18
Letters and volunteering need no voter card

questions.prompt: What does Article 12 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child give children?

options.label: The right to vote from age 16
options.rationale: It's about being heard, not voting.

options.label: The right to stand for parliament
options.rationale: It doesn't cover standing for office.

options.label: The right to express their views in matters affecting them
The right to leave school at any age

questions.explanation: Article 12 gives a child capable of forming views the right to express them freely in all matters affecting them.

questions.prompt: Why is the UK Youth Parliament called real political machinery in miniature?

options.label: Its members are elected by and from 11- to 18-year-olds
It can pass laws that bind the whole country
options.rationale: It campaigns and debates; it doesn't make national law.

options.label: Its members are appointed by MPs
Only people over 18 may take part

questions.explanation: Young people aged 11 to 18 vote and stand in its elections, and members run campaigns: an election system in miniature.

questions.prompt: A 15-year-old writes to her UK MP. Why, by Level 93's rule, is she part of the MP's job?

options.label: Only voters are MPs' concern, so she isn't
options.rationale: MPs represent all the people in the constituency.

options.label: MPs represent everyone who lives in their constituency
Her parents must sign the letter for it to count
Youth Parliament members handle all under-18s instead

questions.explanation: UK MPs represent all the people who live in their constituency, whether or not they voted, and that includes people too young to vote.
